title: Chapter 14: Glossary and Your Next Project
content:
Chapter 14: Glossary and Your Next Project

Return to the glossary when a term becomes unclear. The steps that follow will help you turn one of the book’s projects into work that another developer, reader or client can inspect.

Glossary

Agent

A software system that uses an AI model to work towards a goal. Its design may combine context, tools, memory and decision logic.

AI Assistant

An application that helps a user answer questions, draft material, summarise text or carry out tasks using AI.

API

Application Programming Interface: an interface through which software systems communicate.

API Key

A credential used to authenticate with an API provider. Keep it out of source code and Git history.

Chunk

A portion of a larger document prepared for search, retrieval or processing.

Context

Information supplied to a model for a particular request, such as instructions, conversation history or retrieved passages.

Deployment

Making an application available outside its local development environment.

Embedding

A numerical representation of text that can be compared with other representations for similarity search.

Evaluation

Checking whether an AI system’s outputs meet the requirements of a defined use case.

Guardrail

A rule, validation check or review process intended to constrain an AI system’s behaviour or catch failures.

Hallucination

A model output that presents unsupported or false information, often with apparent confidence.

Human-in-the-Loop

A design in which a person reviews or approves designated outputs or actions.

LLM

Large Language Model: a model used to process and generate text.

Memory

Stored context that an assistant can retrieve for later interactions.

Prompt

The instructions and other input given to a model for a request.

Prompt Template

A reusable prompt with fields that are filled in for each request.

RAG

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieving relevant material and supplying it as context for a generated answer.

Semantic Search

Retrieval based on similarity of meaning, extending beyond exact keyword matching.

Structured Output

Output organised into a specified form, such as JSON, labelled sections or a table.

Token

A unit of text processed by a model. Token counts contribute to context limits and, for many APIs, usage charges.

Tool

A function or external capability made available through the application’s controlled execution logic.

Tool Calling

Using permitted functions or APIs as part of an AI application’s workflow.

Vector Database

A database that stores and searches vector representations, including embeddings.

Suggested Next Steps for the Reader

First, Polish One Project

Choose a project you can explain from input to output. The Personal AI Work Assistant is a useful option if you want to show how retrieval, tools and memory fit together. Finish its README, setup instructions, tests, sample outputs, limitations and deployment notes, then add screenshots and a short portfolio description.

Second, Publish Your Code

Create a repository such as python-ai-work-assistant. Include README.md, requirements.txt, app.py, a placeholder-only .env.example or secrets example, screenshots, tests and labelled sample outputs. Explain the application’s limitations in the README.

Check the repository before making it public. Exclude .env, .streamlit/secrets.toml, API keys, private data, client files, memory.json and logs containing secrets. A working example should not expose the data used to develop it.

Third, Create a Demo Video

Record a short walkthrough using data you can share. Show the application responding to input, and explain any visible failure or limitation instead of editing it into an unsupported success claim.

  1. Show the app homepage.
  2. Ask a general AI question.
  3. Upload a PDF.
  4. Ask a document question.
  5. Use the calculator tool.
  6. Save a memory.
  7. Run the evaluation self-check.
  8. Explain the safety limitations.

Fourth, Write a Case Study

Describe the problem, your solution, the stack and the implemented features. Explain the challenges, what you learned, the safety decisions and the improvements still needed. A title such as Building a Personal AI Work Assistant with Python, RAG, Tools, Memory, and Guardrails tells a reader what the case study covers.

Fifth, Build a Second Version

Choose the next change from the problems observed during testing or use. Possible additions include vector retrieval, better tool routing, database-backed memory, authentication, cost tracking, evaluation reports, deployment logs, user feedback and source citations. Record what changed and compare its behaviour with the earlier version.

Further Learning Paths

The following paths extend different parts of the book. Choose one that supports the application you want to build.

Path 1: Production AI Engineering

Study FastAPI, Docker, PostgreSQL and Redis alongside authentication, background jobs, monitoring, logging and cloud deployment. Apply them to an application with a clear operational requirement.

Path 2: Advanced RAG

Explore hybrid search, metadata filtering, reranking, query expansion and document parsing. Add citation tracking, retrieval evaluation and questions that require material from several documents.

Path 3: Agentic Workflows

Work with tool schemas, planner-executor designs, approval gates, workflow orchestration and state machines. Study multi-agent evaluation and task queues when the workflow needs them.

Path 4: AI Product Development

Practise user interviews, MVP design, pricing, onboarding and analytics. Use feedback and support conversations to improve the workflow, including the way it explains uncertainty and asks for review.

Path 5: Freelance AI Automation

Develop client discovery, service packaging, proposal writing, automation audits and workflow mapping. Include AI tool integration, maintenance responsibilities, maintenance retainers and support terms in your service design.

Closing Message to the Reader

You have a sequence of projects to return to as your needs change: a small assistant, document retrieval, tools, memory, workflows, evaluation and deployment. Pick one, test it with inputs it was not designed around, and write down what happens. Those observations will give you a more useful next task than another feature list.

Thank you for reading Agentic AI With Python. I hope these projects help you build applications you can understand, improve and explain to the people who use them.
